mainEntity.name: How much does a Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine replacement costs between £2,500 and £5,200 supply-only for a rebuilt unit, with fitting adding £600-£1,200 depending on your location and whether you choose a Renault specialist or main dealer. Used H5H 450 or H5H 470 engines can be found from £1,200-£3,000, but come with no warranty and no upgraded components.

mainEntity.name: What are the common signs of timing chain failure in a Renault Captur 1.3 TCE?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common sign is rattling on cold start - a distinct metallic rattle lasting 1-3 seconds after starting the engine. Other signs include engine management light illumination, noticeable loss of power, irregular engine running, and rough idling with vibrations. Early units (2018-2020) are most affected. The 1.3 TCE is generally more reliable than the 1.2 TCE it replaced, but timing chain issues have been reported.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Renault Captur 1.3 TCE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your Captur 1.3 TCE is otherwise sound and has no major body or chassis issues. A 2018-2022 Captur 1.3 TCE values between £6,000 and £16,000, making a £2,500-£5,200 rebuilt engine replacement - around 20-35% of the car's value - a decision that depends on ownership horizon. For older examples under £6,000, evaluate carefully. For higher-value examples over £10,000, replacement is usually justified.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine replacement typically takes 2-5 working days from delivery of the replacement engine. Specialist fitters often complete the work in 2-3 days, while main dealers may take 4-5 days due to scheduling. Mobile fitters offering supply & fit at your location may operate on different turnaround times.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine codes?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Captur 1.3 TCE range includes three main engine codes. H5H 450 (130hp) is the entry-level variant, fitted to Phase 1 models from 2018-2020. H5H 470 (150-155hp) is the mid-range variant, offering stronger performance. H5H 490 (140-160hp with mild hybrid) is the most advanced variant, featuring 12V mild hybrid technology from 2020 onwards. All are 1.3-litre (1,330cc) four-cylinder turbocharged petrol engines.

mainEntity.name: Are Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engines reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H) is widely regarded as a significant improvement over the problematic 1.2 TCE engine. Developed in partnership with Daimler, the 1.3 TCE has received positive reviews for its refinement and reliability. However, early units (pre-2020) can suffer from timing chain wear, and cooling system leaks from the plastic thermostat housing affect all years. Regular oil changes with high-quality synthetic oil and preventative cooling system inspection are essential for longevity.

historyTimeline.h2: Renault Captur 1.3 TCE - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H) was introduced as a modern, efficient petrol engine developed in partnership with Daimler (Mercedes-Benz), replacing the earlier 1.2 TCE which had gained a poor reputation for timing chain issues. Launched in 2018, the 1.3 TCE quickly became the Captur's flagship petrol engine, offering improved power, refinement, and reliability over its predecessor. Available in multiple power outputs from 130hp to 160hp, the H5H engine family has been fitted to both Phase 1 and Phase 2 Captur models, as well as numerous other Renault, Dacia, Nissan and Mercedes vehicles.

milestones.description: 1.3 TCE (H5H) launched in Renault Scenic and Grand Scenic; 115hp, 140hp and 160hp variants
H5H 450 (130hp) introduced in Renault Captur Phase 1
H5H 470 (150-155hp) introduced as higher-output Captur variant
Captur Phase 2 launched with updated 1.3 TCE engine range
H5H 490 (160hp) introduced with mild hybrid technology
Mid-life updates improve timing chain durability and thermal management
Current specification continues with 140hp and 160hp mild hybrid variants

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every 1.3 TCE engine fitted to the Renault Captur is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Renault Captur 1.3 TCE Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H) is widely regarded as a significant improvement over the problematic 1.2 TCE engine it replaced. Developed in partnership with Daimler, the 1.3 TCE has received positive reviews for its refinement, smoothness and power delivery. However, like all modern turbocharged petrol engines, the H5H family has known failure points - particularly timing chain wear on early units (pre-2020) and cooling system leaks from the plastic thermostat housing. Rebuilt engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: Timing Chain Wear - "Why the Renault Captur 1.3 TCE Rattles on Cold Start"
problems.affectedModels: Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H 450, H5H 470, H5H 490, 2018-2020 particularly affected; post-2021 improved)
problems.rootCause: The timing chain can stretch and show signs of wear, particularly on early production units (pre-2020) or vehicles with infrequent oil changes and short-trip urban driving. Symptoms include rattling on cold start, irregular engine running, loss of power, and engine warning light illumination.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: New timing chain kit, tensioner, guides, camshaft sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: Good preventative measure if caught early; pre-2020 units should be inspected at 40,000 miles
When timing chain failure has caused valve or piston damage; often the most cost-effective route on higher-mileage examples

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2018-2022 Renault Captur 1.3 TCE sits in the £6,000-£16,000 value band [THIRD-PARTY, Auto Trader 2025]. A timing chain replacement at £800-£1,400 is good value (8-15% of vehicle value). A full engine replacement at £2,500-£4,200 represents 20-35% of vehicle value - viable if the car is otherwise sound, but evaluate carefully on sub-£6,000 examples.
problems.recommendation: For early (pre-2020) Captur 1.3 TCE models, preventative timing chain inspection and replacement at 40,000-50,000 miles is strongly recommended. Regular oil changes with high-quality synthetic oil meeting Renault's specifications are the best protection against premature chain wear. If the chain has already failed and caused internal damage, a rebuilt engine with upgraded components offers better long-term reliability than attempting to repair a damaged bottom end.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt H5H 450 Renault Captur 1.3 TCE engine prices

problems.h4: Cooling System Leaks - "Why the Renault Captur 1.3 TCE Loses Coolant"
problems.affectedModels: Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H 450, H5H 470, H5H 490, all years)
problems.rootCause: The plastic thermostat housing is prone to cracking and leaking coolant. The water pump can also fail, particularly if incorrect or non-genuine belts are fitted. Symptoms include low coolant levels, engine temperature fluctuations, and in severe cases, overheating.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: New thermostat housing, gaskets, coolant flush
repairOptions.longevity: Good preventative measure; common failure point on all H5H engines

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: New water pump, belt, coolant flush
repairOptions.longevity: If water pump has failed or is leaking; use genuine or OEM-spec parts
If overheating has caused head gasket or internal damage; usually only justified on higher-value examples

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2018-2022 Renault Captur 1.3 TCE sits in the £6,000-£16,000 value band [THIRD-PARTY, Auto Trader 2025]. Thermostat housing replacement at £250-£450 is good value (3-5% of vehicle value). A full engine replacement at £2,500-£4,200 represents 20-35% of vehicle value - evaluate carefully on older examples.
problems.recommendation: The plastic thermostat housing is a known weak point across the H5H engine family. If you notice coolant loss or temperature fluctuations, have the cooling system inspected immediately. Replacing the thermostat housing preventatively at 40,000-50,000 miles is a cost-effective measure. Use only genuine or OEM-spec parts for the water pump to avoid premature failure.

problems.group: Camshaft Oil Control Valve and Oil Consumption
problems.h4: Camshaft Oil Control Valve and Oil Consumption - "Why the Renault Captur 1.3 TCE Uses Oil"
problems.affectedModels: Renault Captur 1.3 TCE (H5H 450, H5H 470, 2018-2020 particularly affected)
problems.rootCause: Camshaft oil control valves can fail on early (pre-2020) units, leading to irregular engine running and higher than normal oil consumption. Oil consumption can also be caused by piston ring wear on higher-mileage examples.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: New oil control valves, oil change
repairOptions.longevity: Good if caught early; pre-2020 units should be inspected regularly

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: New piston rings, cylinder honing, full engine strip
repairOptions.longevity: High-cost repair; often only justified on otherwise sound vehicles
When oil consumption has caused secondary damage or engine is high-mileage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2018-2022 Renault Captur 1.3 TCE sits in the £6,000-£16,000 value band [THIRD-PARTY, Auto Trader 2025]. Oil control valve replacement at £250-£450 is good value. Piston ring replacement at £1,200-£2,200 represents 15-30% of vehicle value - consider full engine replacement if the vehicle is high-mileage.
problems.recommendation: For early (pre-2020) Captur 1.3 TCE models, monitor oil consumption between services. If oil consumption increases noticeably, have the camshaft oil control valves inspected. Regular oil changes with high-quality synthetic oil are essential for preventing premature wear.
